name: Dana Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Dana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union or party, and nothing you say gets your name on it. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm on an overhead distribution crew out of the Eastfield depot, so mostly the poles and wires that run down people's streets. We're in the yard at six thirty, the foreman reads out the jobs, and we're off in the bucket truck by seven. Today was swapping a rotten pole on Mill Lane and hanging a new transformer, which is a good day because you see the thing you built.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the crew and I like that the work is real. If I do it wrong, someone's fridge goes off, or worse, so you pay attention. What wears me out is storm call-outs in winter, sixteen-hour shifts in sleet, and the new tablet the company gave us for job sheets, which freezes every time it gets cold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it out. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say: told you so. Every few months somebody at head office sends round a video about smart this and smart that, and the poles still need climbing. I'd say it in the break room and leave it there, I'm not one for posting online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved. I don't use any of these AI things and I don't want to have to start. If it fizzles out, I get to keep doing the job the way Rob (her foreman) taught me, and that suits me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep working my shifts, keep taking the storm overtime, and keep putting a chunk of every pay into the savings account like I have since my apprenticeship. Maybe I'd finally get my high-voltage switching ticket, but that's been on the list for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like the weather forecast saying a normal week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the tablet freezes. In this picture, would anything about the paperwork side change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the dispatch office gets a computer that sorts out the fault calls quicker, and that's fine by me. As long as I don't have to talk to a chatbot to book my leave, I don't care what they run in the office. The day a computer tells me which pole is safe to climb, I'll start caring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about money? Does anything feel tight right now, apart from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, and I know I'm lucky. Yusuf (my partner) fixes buses and I earn good money with the overtime, so we've got about a year of bills put by. We rent, and the rent keeps going up, but it's not keeping me up at night.

say: I'd tell the crew that the **poles still need climbing**, whatever head office videos promise.
I'd keep it to the **break room** rather than posting anything online.
think: I'm **relieved**, because I never wanted to learn AI tools in the first place.
I'd get to keep doing the job the way **my foreman** taught me.
do: Keep working **normal shifts** and taking the winter storm overtime.
Keep putting **part of every pay** into savings, as I have since my apprenticeship.
Maybe finally sit the **high-voltage switching** ticket I've put off for two years.
feel: **Calm**, like a forecast that promises an ordinary week.
S0.quote: The day a computer tells me which pole is safe to climb, I'll start caring.
fieldNote: Dana defines her job by **physical risk**, and only cares about tech that touches that risk.
She already dislikes the **job-sheet tablet**, so even small digital change irritates her.
Strong savings and a working partner mean **no money pressure** behind her calm.

steps.text: Keep taking winter storm overtime on the Eastfield crew
Put part of each pay into the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office lot who should be worried, not us. They can automate the planning and the parts ordering all they like, someone still has to go up the pole. At work I'd probably moan about whatever new app they make us use, because there will be one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job's safe but my day gets more annoying. More screens, more ticking boxes, a computer checking my job sheets and flagging me if I'm slow. I'm good with my hands, I'm average with forms, and I'm worried I'd look worse on paper than I really am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Rob to put me on the jobs that are pure line work and leave the paperwork-heavy stuff, like new connections, to someone else. I'd sit the switching ticket this year so I've got one more thing a machine can't do. And I'd keep saving, maybe a bit more, just because things feel less settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not scared for my pay, just tired of being told to change things that weren't broken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew or at the depot would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly Pauline (the depot planner) has done the job schedules for twenty years, and that's exactly the kind of work this picture says goes to software. She's brilliant at it. I'd feel bad for her, and honestly a bit worried about who'd sort out our jobs when the computer gets it wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use AI tools. If the depot made the new system compulsory, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd use it, because I'm not losing a good job over an app. But I'd do the bare minimum and I'd get one of the younger lads to show me twice. I won't be the one asking it questions for fun.

say: I'd say the **office staff** should worry, because someone still has to climb the pole.
I'd **moan about** whatever new app the depot makes us use.
think: My **job is safe**, but my day fills up with more screens and box-ticking.
I worry a computer checking my job sheets would make me **look slower** than I am.
do: Ask my foreman for **pure line work** and fewer paperwork-heavy connection jobs.
Sit the **switching ticket** this year so I have another skill a machine lacks.
Save **a bit more**, because things feel less settled.
feel: **Uneasy**, though not scared for my pay.
**Tired** of changing things that weren't broken.
S1.quote: Pauline (the depot planner) has done the job schedules for twenty years, and that's exactly the kind of work this picture says goes to software.
fieldNote: Dana sees the threat in the **office**, and her sympathy goes first to the planner.
Her private worry is being **measured by software**, not replaced by it.
She would comply with new systems but **minimally**, leaning on younger colleagues.

steps.text: Ask the foreman for straight line work over new-connection paperwork
Sit the high-voltage switching ticket this year
Raise monthly savings while the depot reorganises

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's ridiculous, and I'd mean it, at least at first. Two years is nothing, nobody's ready. At work I'd say the union and the company will have to sort it out, because we're the ones keeping the lights on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the thinking part of my job is small, so 2028 doesn't scare me much. It's 2031 that does. If a robot can climb a pole and splice a cable as well as me, then I've got about five years left of the only work I know. I'm not someone who changes easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd stop spending on anything big and push my savings harder, maybe two years of bills instead of one. In the first year after AGI arrives, I'd sign up for every safety and robot-handling course the company offers, even though I'd hate it, because the people who supervise the machines will be the last ones kept. And I'd talk to Yusuf about whether we stay renting or buy somewhere cheap outright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a knot in my stomach. I've got money, so it's not panic, but I don't have a plan B and I don't want one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture 2031, when those robots arrive. What does your crew look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe two of us and a machine, instead of four of us. One person to watch the robot and one to sign off the work, and I'd want to be one of those two. The other two would be the ones with the least time in, and I'm only five years in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be about 32 then. What would you be doing instead, if it came to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I really don't know, and that's the bit that bothers me. My dad drove a forklift, my mum cleaned offices, nobody in my family has ever done a desk job. Maybe I'd follow Yusuf into fixing machines, because something will have to fix the robots.

say: I'd call it **ridiculous**, because two years is nothing and nobody's ready.
I'd say the **union and company** must sort it out, since we keep the lights on.
think: The thinking side of my job is small, so **2028** barely scares me.
**2031** does, because robots that climb and splice leave me about five years of work.
do: Push savings to **two years of bills** and stop any big spending now.
Take every **robot-handling course** the company offers once AGI arrives.
Talk with my partner about **buying somewhere cheap** outright instead of renting.
feel: **Anxious**, a knot in my stomach, though not panic thanks to savings.
S2.quote: If a robot can climb a pole and splice a cable as well as me, then I've got about five years left of the only work I know.
fieldNote: Dana clearly separates the **2028** thinking wave from the **2031** robot wave.
She fears being cut as **junior on the crew**, not the technology itself.
She would retrain only **reluctantly**, choosing supervisory courses as a survival move.

steps.text: Build savings up to two years of household bills
Sign up for company robot-handling and safety courses
Decide with Yusuf whether to buy a cheap flat outright

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's not panic. I'd tell the newer apprentices to get their tickets while they still mean something. Publicly I'd sound pretty steady about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's the same end point, just later. Robots around 2034 means I'd be about 35, still young enough to start over but old enough that I'd hate it. I'd probably spend those years telling myself it won't really happen to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the switching ticket and then the substation one, because substation work has more checks and rules, and I think they'd keep people there longest. I'd keep saving like mad. And I'd keep my head down and work hard, because when they choose who to keep, being reliable for ten years should count for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a slower kind. Knowing about the robots five years out feels like knowing a storm's coming next week instead of tonight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the extra three years compared with the fast one change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly I'd be able to save more first. Five years of storm overtime is a lot of money, and I could have most of a house paid for. The fast one gives me no time to get anything solid under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep your head down. Is that a plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both, if I'm honest. Working hard and being reliable is what I know how to do, so that's my plan. Whether it's enough when a robot doesn't need sleep, I really can't say.

say: I'd tell people we have **a few years**, so there's no need to panic.
I'd urge the **new apprentices** to get their tickets while they still count.
think: It's the **same end point**, only later, with robots arriving when I'm about 35.
I'd probably spend the years **telling myself** it won't really reach us.
do: Finish the switching ticket, then the **substation** ticket, where people may stay longest.
Keep **saving hard** from storm overtime toward most of a house.
Work hard and stay **reliable**, hoping a long record counts.
feel: **Anxious**, but slower, like a storm forecast for next week.
S3.quote: Knowing about the robots five years out feels like knowing a storm's coming next week instead of tonight.
fieldNote: The extra time matters to Dana mostly as **more savings**, not as time to change careers.
She admits her plan is **part hope**, resting on reliability over skills.
Substation work appeals because she sees **rules and checks** as protection.

steps.text: Finish the switching ticket, then the substation ticket
Put five years of storm overtime toward a house deposit
Keep working full shifts and building a clean safety record

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and loads can change before then. I'd probably say it with a shrug, like people say it about the weather. Nobody in the break room would argue with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd mostly ignore it for the first few years, if I'm honest. That's how I am, I don't move until I have to. The thinking AI in 2036 hardly touches me, so the real date is 2039, and I'd be nearly 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I do, keep saving, and buy a place with Yusuf in the next couple of years so we're not paying rent when it hits. Somewhere around year five I'd probably finally do a proper course, maybe electrical maintenance for the machines. But I wouldn't do anything dramatic early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's on my mind but it's not shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you think about leaving lines work before the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not leaving, no. I like the work and I'd want to be there as long as it lasts. Ten years of good pay is ten years of good pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a 17-year-old cousin who wanted to become a lineworker in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my cousin Amira to do the electrical side too, not just the climbing. Do the job, yes. If you know how the whole system works, you're useful whoever or whatever is up the pole.

say: I'd shrug and say **ten years** is a long time and loads can change.
Nobody in the **break room** would argue with that.
think: I'd mostly **ignore it** for the first few years, because I move only when I must.
The real date for me is **2039**, when I'd be nearly forty.
do: Keep working and saving, and **buy a place** with my partner within two years.
Take a proper **maintenance course** around year five, not before.
Avoid anything **dramatic** in the early years.
feel: **Uneasy**, with the worry on my mind but quiet.
S4.quote: I'd tell my cousin Amira to do the electrical side too, not just the climbing.
fieldNote: With a decade, Dana's **resistance** shows plainly: she would wait until about year five.
She would use the time for **buying a home**, a life step rather than a career change.
Her advice to her cousin shows she knows **system knowledge** outlasts climbing.

steps.text: Buy a flat with Yusuf within two years to stop paying rent
Keep the same crew job and storm overtime for now
Enrol in an electrical maintenance course around year five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, because of the robots three years later. I'd have no time to get a house sorted or learn something else. What would help is the company being honest early about which jobs go, and paying for proper retraining while we're still on full wages, not after we're let go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who goes up first when something goes wrong. A robot might do a clean job on a sunny day, but storm work at three in the morning, with trees down and lines arcing, is a different animal. I'd want someone to ask whether the robots can do that before they decide we're not needed.

headlineQuote: A robot might do a clean job on a sunny day, but storm work at three in the morning, with trees down and lines arcing, is a different animal.
portrait: Dana is a 27-year-old **overhead lineworker** on a distribution crew who lives with her bus-mechanic partner.
She has **strong savings**, rents, and likes work she can see and touch.
She avoids new tech and **never uses AI**, and sees office jobs as the ones at risk.
Her worry grows only with **robots that climb**, peaking in the fast 2028 picture.
Her plans are **saving, buying a home** and reluctant courses, mostly later rather than sooner.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots by 2031 leave no time to buy a home or retrain.
whatWouldHelp: The company being **honest early** about which jobs go.
**Paid retraining** while crews are still on full wages.
